prompt: In laymen's terms, what does it mean to be Turing complete?
judge_reasoning: Candidate 1 directly and accurately explains Turing completeness as the ability to simulate any Turing machine, in clear lay terms. Candidate 2 is also mostly correct, but it drifts into overconfident real-world claims (e.g., “learn and improve”) and implies more than Turing completeness alone guarantees. Candidate 3 includes a misleading factual claim about a “Turing Completeness Test” and gives an oversimplified criterion list. Candidate 4 has several conceptual inaccuracies/overstatements (e.g., “not Turing complete” based on getting stuck on particular problems and stating cryptology requires Turing completeness), though it still gestures toward the right idea.
